passages.t: A song for the king, and ‘Your throne, O God’
passages.happening:
This psalm is a wedding song. The heading calls it “A love song” and sets it to a tune called “The Lilies” (verse 1). The poet says, “My heart is stirred by a noble theme as I recite my verses to the king; my tongue is the pen of a skillful writer” (verse 1).

He praises the king. “You are the most handsome of men; grace has anointed your lips” (verse 2). He calls him to ride out “on behalf of truth and humility and justice” (verse 4).

Then comes the line that has puzzled readers ever since. “Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever, and justice is the scepter of Your kingdom” (verse 6). The next verse speaks to the king again: “therefore God, your God, has anointed you above your companions with the oil of joy” (verse 7).

The king is dressed in robes scented with spices. Music plays in “palaces of ivory”, and the queen stands at his right hand in gold (verses 8 and 9).
passages.hearers:
A royal wedding was a matter of state. It could seal a bond between two kingdoms. The court poet was a kind of singer for great days.

Which king is not said. Solomon is a common guess, because he married foreign princesses and was rich. Others think the song was used at more than one royal wedding. The text does not let anyone name the day.

The book page counts Psalm 45 among the royal psalms and explains how Jews and Christians read them. Anointing with oil marked a king as chosen by God. ‘Ophir’ was a far-off place famous for gold (1 Kings 9:28). Carved ivory was a sign of great wealth.

The first hearers would also have heard the king's duty. He rides out for truth, humility and justice. A king who loved righteousness and hated wickedness (verse 7) was the king God wanted.
passages.later:
The letter to the Hebrews quotes verses 6 and 7. “But about the Son He says: ‘Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever’” (Hebrews 1:8). The writer reads the words as spoken to Jesus, and uses them to show that the Son is greater than the angels.

Notice that Hebrews keeps both halves. The Son is called ‘God’, and yet “God, Your God, has anointed You” (Hebrews 1:9). Christians have seen here, in a small space, what the church later called the Trinity: the Son is God, and he is not the Father.

Isaiah also spoke of a royal child who would be called “Mighty God” (Isaiah 9:6).
passages.hard:
How should verse 6 be read? Is a human king really called God? Here it is honest to say that translators differ.

The Hebrew most naturally reads ‘Your throne, O God’, as words to the king, and most English Bibles print it that way. Some scholars say this was court language. The king stood for God, and the Hebrew word elohim is sometimes used of human rulers or judges. The same word is put into English as “the judges” in one law (Exodus 21:6). Other translations avoid calling the king God, with readings such as ‘your divine throne’ or ‘your throne is from God’. These are harder to get from the Hebrew, but careful scholars hold them.

Jewish readers have read the line in more than one way: as words to the king, or as words to God himself. An old Aramaic translation used by Jews, the Targum, speaks to the king of this psalm as the anointed one, the word that gives us ‘Messiah’.

Christians read it, with Hebrews, as fitting Jesus fully. Many also grant that the first singer may have meant something smaller, which later history filled out. Both readings are held in good faith.
passages.asks:
Before the wedding, before the gold, the poet praises the king for truth, humility and justice. That is what makes a ruler good in God's eyes.

Christians who read this psalm of Jesus are asked to see him the same way: beautiful, gracious in speech, and fighting for the humble. What kind of king do you picture when you pray?

passages.t: ‘Listen, O daughter’: the bride and the procession
passages.happening:
Now the poet turns to the bride. “Listen, O daughter! Consider and incline your ear: Forget your people and your father’s house” (verse 10). The king desires her beauty (verse 11). Rich people, even from the city of Tyre, come with gifts (verse 12).

Then the procession. “All glorious is the princess in her chamber; her gown is embroidered with gold” (verse 13). “In colorful garments she is led to the king” (verse 14), and her companions follow “with joy and gladness” (verse 15).

The song ends with a blessing on the king. His sons will take the place of his fathers. “I will commemorate your name through all generations” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
A princess who married a foreign king left her home for good. ‘Forget your people’ was not cruel advice. It named what the marriage would cost her. She would belong now to a new people and a new house.

Tyre was a rich trading city on the coast to the north, in what is now Lebanon. ‘The Daughter of Tyre’ is a poetic way of naming the city. Gifts from Tyre showed that foreign powers wanted the new queen's favour.

‘Bow to him, for he is your lord’ (verse 11) describes a royal court. Everyone bowed to a king, his queen included. The psalm describes a wedding in its own world. What the New Testament says about marriage is a different passage (Ephesians 5:21-33), and churches understand it in different ways.
passages.later:
Ruth made the same kind of choice as this bride when she said to Naomi, “your people will be my people, and your God will be my God” (Ruth 1:16).

The prophets pictured God as the husband of his people. The New Testament speaks of the church as the bride of Christ. Paul wrote, “I promised you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2). The Bible ends at a wedding: “For the marriage of the Lamb has come, and His bride has made herself ready” (Revelation 19:7). Christians have long read Psalm 45 as a picture of that wedding.
passages.asks:
The bride is asked to leave something behind for the sake of someone she loves. Following Christ is pictured in the same way in the New Testament. It is not only giving up. It is being brought in ‘with joy and gladness’.

If you read this psalm as a picture of Christ and his people, notice who the beauty belongs to. The king desires the bride. You are wanted, not just put up with.
